summary: An informational memo describing how codecs registered in Microsoft's WAVE and AVI registries can be referenced from the IANA namespace by Internet applications.

plainLanguage.summary: A name list so internet programs can refer to the sound and video formats used on Windows.

questions: how do i identify avi codecs
subtitle: How Internet applications can reference Microsoft's historical audio and video codecs.

tldr.problem: Millions of audio (WAVE) and video (AVI) files use codec formats originally registered by Microsoft. Internet applications (RTP, RTSP, SDP) need a standard way to identify which codec was used to encode a file, but Microsoft's registry numbers were not part of the IANA namespace.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a mapping: WAVE audio codecs are referenced as 'audio/vnd.wave; codec=XXX' where XXX is the hexadecimal WAVE Format ID, and AVI video codecs as 'video/vnd.avi; codec=YYY' where YYY is the FourCC code. The RFC lists all registered codecs as of January 1998 and shows how to convert them to GUID values for use in Microsoft's Advanced Streaming Format.
tldr.outcome: Internet protocols can now identify legacy media codecs, enabling applications to correctly decode files created before IPv6 and RTP were widespread. The registry is stable and historical, maintained as a reference.

today: RFC 2361 is Informational and describes the registries as they stood in 1998. WAVE and AVI file formats are still used for legacy media content. The GUID mapping is used in systems that need to decode these older formats or maintain compatibility with content created in the 1990s and early 2000s.

sections.title: The Legacy Media Problem
sections.content:
Internet applications increasingly need to reference multimedia content. For new content created specifically for the Internet (using RTP, RTSP, or SDP), this is straightforward. But the vast majority of existing multimedia content was created for Windows: WAVE audio files and AVI video files with codecs registered in Microsoft's own registry.

Internet protocols need a way to identify these legacy codecs without creating parallel registries or breaking compatibility. The RFC solves this by registering Microsoft's codec namespaces within the IANA vendor tree, allowing Internet applications to reference Microsoft codecs using standard IANA identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the internet was big, companies like Microsoft made their own media formats. Now internet programs need to understand those old formats, so we need a translation guide.

sections.title: The IANA Vendor Tree Mechanism
sections.content:
The IANA namespace includes a vendor tree for formats registered by non-IANA registries. A vendor tree entry is identified as 'vnd.RegistryName'. Within that namespace, a specific codec is referenced by a required 'codec' parameter, as specified in RFC 2048 (MIME registration procedures).

For WAVE audio: audio/vnd.wave; codec=XXX, where XXX is the WAVE Format ID in hexadecimal. For AVI video: video/vnd.avi; codec=YYY, where YYY is the AVI Codec ID (a FourCC 32-bit code). Both registries are maintained by Microsoft as a free service and have been stable for years.
sections.plainLanguage: The system lets internet programs say 'audio/vnd.wave; codec=1' to mean 'the PCM codec from Microsoft's WAVE registry'.

sections.title: WAVE Audio Codecs
sections.content:
The WAVE registry contains audio codec identifiers as 16-bit hexadecimal values called WAVE Format IDs (or WAVE form Registration Numbers). The RFC lists all registered WAVE codecs as of January 1998, including common formats like PCM (codec 1), Microsoft ADPCM (codec 2), IEEE floating-point (codec 3), and many others from vendors such as Compaq, IBM, Intel, OKI, Dialogic, Yamaha, and DSP solutions.

Each entry includes the codec name, the hexadecimal Format ID, the IANA namespace identifier (for example, 'audio/vnd.wave;codec=1' for PCM), and contact information for the original registrant. The registry is historic; contact information reflects original entries and may be outdated.
sections.plainLanguage: Microsoft has a big list of sound codec numbers. Each number means 'this file uses this type of compression'.

sections.title: AVI Video Codecs and FourCC Codes
sections.content:
The AVI registry uses a different encoding for codecs: FourCC codes, which are 32-bit values representing four ASCII characters (case-sensitive). Examples include 'H260' (for H.260 video compression), 'SCRN' (for screen capture), and many others registered by vendors such as Intel, Microsoft, and various compression technology companies.

AVI codecs are referenced in the IANA namespace as 'video/vnd.avi; codec=YYY' where YYY is the FourCC code. The same GUID conversion mechanism applies: the FourCC code is converted to a hexadecimal 32-bit value and inserted into the GUID template used by Microsoft's Advanced Streaming Format.
sections.plainLanguage: Video codes are four-letter names, like 'DIVX' or 'H260'. Internet programs need to know what those mean.

sections.title: GUID Mapping and Advanced Streaming Format
sections.content:
Both WAVE Format IDs and FourCC codes have defined mappings to GUID (Globally Unique Identifier) values. GUIDs, also known as UUIDs, are 128-bit identifiers standardized by the Open Software Foundation. They use the template {XXXXXXXX-0000-0010-8000-00AA00389B71}, where XXXXXXXX is the hexadecimal codec value.

For a WAVE Format ID like 123, the GUID becomes {00000123-0000-0010-8000-00AA00389B71}. For a FourCC like 'H260', the ASCII characters are converted to a 32-bit hex value (30363248 in this case), yielding {30363248-0000-0010-8000-00AA00389B71}. This mapping enables systems using GUID-based approaches (such as Microsoft's Advanced Streaming Format) to directly reference these legacy codec values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each codec number can be converted into a much longer unique identifier that computers use internally. The conversion formula is the same for all codecs.
